newsitem.title: UK: Britain tells Sinn Fein to deliver IRA ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Britain tells Sinn Fein to deliver IRA ceasefire.

text.p: Britain told Sinn Fein on Monday to stop lecturing about disarmament and step up efforts to deliver an IRA ceasefire.

In a further sign of mounting pressure on the Irish Republican Army to end violence, Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam dismissed protests from its political arm Sinn Fein that the province's peace process is being stymied by demands for scrapping arms.
"I think Sinn Fein ought to be concentrating on giving me an unequivocal ceasefire before they tell me what else I should be doing," she told reporters in Londonderry city.

Mowlam, the minister charged with trying to steer Northern Ireland through a potentially explosive summer season of parades by pro-British Protestants, said she was heartened that the first march in Bellaghy on Sunday had gone off peacefully.

She was in Londonderry meeting Catholic objectors to the annual parades, as part of a series of talks with both sides. Police kept the peace in Bellaghy when 500 officers formed a buffer zone to keep rival Protestant and Catholic demonstrators apart.
The IRA's murder of two police patrolmen last week, which was followd by two suspected Protestant bomb attacks on Catholics has darkened hopes of political progress.
The killings also increased fears of sectarian violence during the usually volatile marching season.
"I thought Bellaghy was a common sense decision by both sides...I thought Bellaghy was a good omen, because it has not been easy there," Mowlam said.
Her call for an IRA ceasefire, adding fuel to Anglo-Irish and U.S. demands, came on the eve of an attempt by London and Dublin to break the deadlock over arms decommissioning.

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who severed low-level contacts with Sinn Fein last week after the IRA killings, is expected to make a parliamentary statement on Wednesday about terms for Sinn Fein entry to talks, based on an end to violence.

On Tuesday government representatives are expected to present a joint British-Irish paper at round-table talks in Belfast to get around the impasse about how decommissioning can be achieved if the IRA calls a truce.

Political sources in Belfast say the plan is likely to mirror proposals by the talks chairman, former U.S.senator George Mitchell, for the issue to be tackled alongside negotiations on other political matters.
Mowlam said Britain and Ireland were working very hard to reach an agreement which would be discussed in the talks.
Sinn Fein is barred from the multi-party discussions because the IRA refuses to restore a truce it broke in February 1996.
Earlier Martin McGuinness, chief negotiator for Sinn Fein, said the disarmament issue remained a major stumbling block in peace efforts.
He said Sinn Fein wanted an end to violence in the province and the start of real peace negotiations.

"We are working day and night...trying to move the situation forward, and to convince the British government and others that the decommissioning issue which has blocked this process must be removed as an obstacle to forward movement," he told BBC radio.
Republicans said the IRA will not call a ceasefire if they suspect the negotiations will be turned into a "decommissioning conference".
Britain said it will not permit Sinn Fein and the IRA to hold the peace process to ransom.
